Sources are in the shape BE-11 retrieves. Injury-note sources are sourced (never team-guidance) sections of rag/notes, built by parseNote and noteChunks, with the section's first Sources URL as url. sources.title: Training around an injured or recovering knee: Rebuilding knee strength
sources.content: Training around an injured or recovering knee. Rebuilding knee strength: Strong muscles around a damaged knee can help support the joint by taking over some of its work, and leg resistance exercises two to three times a week are a common target. Two starting exercises: a straight-leg raise, lying down and slowly raising the straight leg 6 to 10 inches off the floor; and a half squat, slowly lowering the hips about 10 inches, as if sitting down into a chair.

sources.title: Training around an injured or recovering knee: Warming up and progressing
sources.content: Training around an injured or recovering knee. Warming up and progressing: A warm-up of 5 to 10 minutes of low-impact activity, like walking or riding a stationary bike, comes before the exercises. An exercise shouldn't cause pain. A lighter weight that allows a greater number of reps is gentler on the joint than a heavy one.

sources.title: Training around an injured or recovering knee: When to get checked
sources.content: Training around an injured or recovering knee. When to get checked: Get emergency care straight away after an injury if you heard a crack, the knee looks misshapen, it is numb or tingling, or the skin is blue, grey or cold. Get urgent medical advice if the knee is very painful, you can't move it or put any weight on it, it is badly swollen or has changed shape, it locks, gives way or clicks painfully (painless clicking is normal), or you have a very high temperature or feel hot, cold or shivery and there's redness or heat around the knee. See a doctor if knee pain does not improve within a few weeks.

sources.title: Training around a sore or recovering shoulder: Keep it moving
sources.content: Training around a sore or recovering shoulder. Keep it moving: Staying active and gently moving the shoulder helps, while avoiding things that seem to make it worse. Stopping using the shoulder completely isn't recommended, and neither is slouching when sitting. Making up strenuous exercises or using heavy gym equipment is best avoided with shoulder pain. Recovery can take 6 months or longer.

sources.title: Training around a sore or recovering shoulder: Strengthen the rotator cuff
sources.content: Training around a sore or recovering shoulder. Strengthen the rotator cuff: Resistance band rotations are done with the elbow pressed into the side: internal rotation brings the arm across the body, external rotation rotates it outward. They usually start at 3 sets of 8. A standing row, squeezing the shoulder blades together, works the upper back.

sources.title: Training around a sore or recovering shoulder: When to get checked
sources.content: Training around a sore or recovering shoulder. When to get checked: Get emergency care straight away after an injury if you heard a crack, the shoulder has changed shape or is pointing at an odd angle, the arm is numb, tingling or has pins and needles, or the skin has turned blue or grey or is cold to touch. Get urgent medical advice for sudden or very bad shoulder pain, if you can't move your arm, the arm or shoulder has changed shape or is badly swollen, pins and needles don't go away, there's no feeling in the arm or shoulder, it is hot or cold to touch, the pain started after an injury or accident like a fall, both shoulders are severely painful, or you feel feverish or unwell. See a doctor if shoulder pain is getting worse or does not improve after 2 weeks, or it's very difficult to move the arm or shoulder.

sources.title: Returning to lifting after lower back pain: Keep moving
sources.content: Returning to lifting after lower back pain. Keep moving: Staying active and carrying on with daily activities helps more than bed rest. Bed rest for longer than a day can slow recovery. Walking, swimming, yoga and pilates may also help.

sources.title: Returning to lifting after lower back pain: The first weeks
sources.content: Returning to lifting after lower back pain. The first weeks: Activities that involve heavy lifting or twisting of the back are usually avoided for the first 6 weeks after the pain begins. Starting exercises too soon after an injury can make the pain worse.

sources.title: Returning to lifting after lower back pain: When to get checked
sources.content: Returning to lifting after lower back pain. When to get checked: Get emergency care straight away for back pain with pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs, loss of feeling around the genitals or bottom, changes in the bladder or bowels (such as trouble peeing, or peeing or pooing yourself), changes in how the genitals feel during sex or in sexual function, chest pain, or pain that started after a serious accident such as a car crash. Get urgent medical advice for severe pain that starts suddenly or is getting worse quickly, or if you feel hot, cold, shivery or generally unwell. See a GP if the pain hasn't improved after a few weeks of looking after it at home, it's stopping you doing day-to-day activities, you're worried or struggling to cope, you've lost weight without trying, there's a lump or swelling in the back or it has changed shape, it doesn't ease with rest or is worse at night, it's worse when sneezing, coughing or pooing, or the pain is between the shoulders rather than in the lower back.

sources.title: Training around a sprained or injured ankle or foot: Putting weight on it
sources.content: Training around a sprained or injured ankle or foot. Putting weight on it: Once those first days have passed and the pain and swelling start to settle, weight usually goes back on gradually. Early weight bearing as tolerated is typically recommended: only as much weight on the foot as is comfortable at first, slowly working up to full weight, and walking on it as soon and as much as you are able, under a provider's guidance. Crutches may help at first. If the ankle begins to hurt, that's a sign to stop and rest.

sources.title: Training around a sprained or injured ankle or foot: When to get checked
sources.content: Training around a sprained or injured ankle or foot. When to get checked: Get emergency care straight away after an injury if you heard a crack, the ankle or foot has changed shape or is pointing at an odd angle, it is numb, tingling or has pins and needles, or the skin has turned blue or grey or is cold to touch. Get urgent medical advice if you can't put any weight on it or walk more than a few steps, it's very painful or the pain is getting worse, there's a lot of swelling or bruising or it's getting worse, it feels very stiff or is hard to move, it isn't feeling any better after treating it yourself, or you also have a very high temperature or feel hot, cold or shivery, which could be an infection. See a doctor if the ankle is still swollen or painful after several weeks of self-care, to rule out a severe sprain or a fracture. It's also worth clearing cycling or swimming with a healthcare provider before starting.

sources.title: Training around an injured or sore wrist: Why it's worth getting checked
sources.content: Training around an injured or sore wrist. Why it's worth getting checked: The wrist is a complex system that relies heavily on ligaments for stability. An unrecognised (occult) fracture can be mistaken for a mild or moderate sprain, so pain and swelling that last more than 48 hours are worth seeing a doctor about. A wrist that might be broken isn't something to treat yourself.

sources.title: Training around an injured or sore wrist: When to get checked
sources.content: Training around an injured or sore wrist. When to get checked: Get urgent medical advice if you think the wrist might be broken, or for severe wrist pain, if you heard a snap, grinding or popping noise when it happened, you can't move the wrist or hold things, it has changed shape or colour, you have lost the feeling in part or all of the hand, there's a lump on the wrist that is very painful, hot or red, or you feel faint, dizzy or sick from the pain, or unwell, hot, cold or shivery. See a doctor if the pain is stopping normal activities, is getting worse or keeps coming back, pain and swelling last more than 2 days, the wrist hasn't improved after 2 weeks of home care, there's any tingling or loss of sensation in the hand or wrist, the wrist is painful, warm, swollen and stiff, you feel unwell with a high temperature, or you have diabetes, since hand problems can be more serious with diabetes. A wrist "sprain" can hide a fracture.

sources.title: Bodyweight Squat
sources.content: Bodyweight Squat. A beginner strength exercise (compound, push movement) using body only. Primary muscles: quadriceps. Secondary muscles: glutes, hamstrings. How to: Stand with your feet shoulder width apart. You can place your hands behind your head. This will be your starting position. Begin the movement by flexing your knees and hips, sitting back with your hips. Continue down to full depth if you are able,and quickly reverse the motion until you return to the starting position. As you squat, keep your head and chest up and push your knees out.

sources.title: Dumbbell Rear Lunge
sources.content: Dumbbell Rear Lunge. A intermediate strength exercise (compound, push movement) using dumbbell. Primary muscles: quadriceps. Secondary muscles: calves, glutes, hamstrings. How to: Stand with your torso upright holding two dumbbells in your hands by your sides. This will be your starting position. Step backward with your right leg around two feet or so from the left foot and lower your upper body down, while keeping the torso upright and maintaining balance. Inhale as you go down. Tip: As in the other exercises, do not allow your knee to go forward beyond your toes as you come down, as this will put undue stress on the knee joint. Make sure that you keep your front shin perpendicular to the ground. Keep the torso upright during the lunge; flexible hip flexors are important. A long lunge emphasizes the Gluteus Maximus; a short lunge emphasizes Quadriceps. Push up and go back to the starting position as you exhale. Tip: Use the ball of your feet to push in order to accentuate the quadriceps. To focus on the glutes, press with your heels. Now repeat with the opposite leg.

sources.title: Bodyweight Walking Lunge
sources.content: Bodyweight Walking Lunge. A beginner strength exercise (compound, push movement) using no equipment. Primary muscles: quadriceps. Secondary muscles: calves, glutes, hamstrings. How to: Begin standing with your feet shoulder width apart and your hands on your hips. Step forward with one leg, flexing the knees to drop your hips. Descend until your rear knee nearly touches the ground. Your posture should remain upright, and your front knee should stay above the front foot. Drive through the heel of your lead foot and extend both knees to raise yourself back up. Step forward with your rear foot, repeating the lunge on the opposite leg.

sources.title: Hamstring Stretch
sources.content: Hamstring Stretch. A beginner stretching exercise (isolation, static movement) using no equipment. Primary muscles: hamstrings. How to: Lie on your back with one leg extended above you, with the hip at ninety degrees. Keep the other leg flat on the floor. Loop a belt, band, or rope over the ball of your foot. This will be your starting position. Pull on the belt to create tension in the calves and hamstrings. Hold this stretch for 10-30 seconds, and repeat with the other leg.

sources.title: Pushups
sources.content: Pushups. A beginner strength exercise (compound, push movement) using body only. Primary muscles: chest. Secondary muscles: shoulders, triceps. How to: Lie on the floor face down and place your hands about 36 inches apart while holding your torso up at arms length. Next, lower yourself downward until your chest almost touches the floor as you inhale. Now breathe out and press your upper body back up to the starting position while squeezing your chest. After a brief pause at the top contracted position, you can begin to lower yourself downward again for as many repetitions as needed.

sources.title: Incline Push-Up
sources.content: Incline Push-Up. A beginner strength exercise (compound, push movement) using body only. Primary muscles: chest. Secondary muscles: shoulders, triceps. How to: Stand facing bench or sturdy elevated platform. Place hands on edge of bench or platform, slightly wider than shoulder width. Position forefoot back from bench or platform with arms and body straight. Arms should be perpendicular to body. Keeping body straight, lower chest to edge of box or platform by bending arms. Push body up until arms are extended. Repeat.

sources.title: Answer to 'Legs wrecked after first squat day?'
sources.content: Totally normal after a new routine. Mine faded after about three days. Light cycling and an easy walk the next day helped more than sitting still.

sources.title: Answer to 'Curls or push-ups first?'
sources.content: I put the big movement first while I'm fresh, so push-ups before curls. Arms are less tired for the compound work that way.
